body.text: Australia’s working holidaymaker program “allows young adults to have a twelve-month holiday during which they undertake short-term work and study”. That, at least, is the Home Affairs spin.
But the government’s shambolic attempts to rein in the “backpacker” program remind us that it long ago morphed into a de facto labour scheme for regional and remote Australia.

Initiated in 1975 as a reciprocal arrangement limited to Canada, the UK and Ireland, the program rolled along slowly over its first three decades collecting another fifteen partner countries. Then, in 2005, it changed gears, after the Howard government offered backpackers an inducement to do seasonal work on farms. Now, anyone who completed three months harvest work would be eligible for a second twelve-month visa.
This change sparked spectacular growth in a program that now takes in fifty countries. Within a few years, the number of working holidaymakers in Australia more than doubled.

Over time, the “specified work” to qualify for a second visa was broadened from picking fruit and vegetables to employment in hospitality, fishing, pearling, forestry, mining, construction and disaster recovery. For several major source countries, the age at which someone remained a “young adult” was lifted from thirty to thirty-five.

Then, in 2019, the Morrison government added the option of a third visa in return for a further six months’ work. Two years later, under a free-trade deal signed with Boris Johnson, Morrison agreed that British backpackers could stay for three years without doing any work at all in regional or remote Australia.

Working holidaymaker numbers dropped sharply during the Covid pandemic, but were turbocharged by the third visa option and the concessions to the UK once borders reopened. By June 2026, 226,000 working holidaymakers were in Australia, two-thirds more than before Covid hit. Rapid growth in the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility, or PALM, scheme added a further 24,000 full-time workers to Australia’s rural labour market.

As home affairs minister Tony Burke cast around for ways to cut net overseas migration and counter the rise of One Nation, the working holiday program seemed an obvious target. In July, without any public announcement, he directed his department to restrict new arrivals by pausing working holiday applications from certain countries and slowing down processing from others, including the UK.

Then, in his delayed September speech to the National Press Club, he announced that in future working holidaymakers would have to enter a ballot to secure a second or third visa as well as doing specific work. He set annual caps of 45,000 and 5000 places respectively. Given that Home Affairs granted about 57,000 second and 31,000 third-year visas in 2025–26, the new rules would have forced a significant reduction in numbers.

Burke’s attempt to curb numbers shattered on the rocks of farming and tourist industries heavily reliant on this transient workforce. This week he lifted the cap on third visas to 25,000 places but also increased the work requirement for a second visa from three months to four.

Meanwhile, Anthony Albanese is trying to convince his British counterpart, Andy Burnham, to agree to a winding back of the concessions granted to UK backpackers under the trade deal. But the latest changes increase complexity in the scheme without necessarily achieving the government’s aims.

As ANU economist Stephen Howes argues, it’s very hard to predict the behavioural response of backpackers to the proposed rules. Will the risk of missing out in the ballot deter young travellers from working in regional Australia altogether? If so, then industry opposition will resurface, along with Coalition and One Nation arguments that Labor ignores the concerns of regional Australians. But if the ballot fails to make a significant dent in working holiday numbers, then the government will have taken a political hit without the payoff of cutting migration.

At one point, Burke suggested rural employers should replace backpackers with PALM workers. The more closely regulated PALM scheme was the “preferred agriculture visa,” he said, implying that some rural employers chose backpackers because they were easier to exploit. This offended the farming sector, but it’s a reminder of the sordid history of the working holiday program — exposed in 2015 by Four Corners and declared a national disgrace by a Senate committee the following year — which has been identified as a serious problem in several subsequent inquiries and reports.

New research from the Migrant Justice Institute once again confirms that working holidaymakers put up with underpayment and other abuses because they need employers to sign off on their three months of specified work. Stretching the time to four months increases that employer leverage.
As migration analyst Fergus Peace comments, Burke’s latest changes “bring more compulsion and exploitation to the working holiday program, and more long-term temporariness to the migration system.”

Another route was open to Burke. He could have revoked the third working holidaymaker visa, while also trying to wind back concessions to Britons under the UK trade deal. Backpacker numbers would probably have fallen back to pre-Covid levels, but with the added rural labour force already delivered by a larger PALM scheme.

That change would have been simpler to administer and easier to explain and defend: the public wants us to bring down net overseas migration, the government could say, and we are responding. Both measures — tightening the third visa and the UK concessions — could be sheeted home to Coalition mistakes. Simultaneously, the government could have promoted the further expansion of PALM, emphasising its diplomatic and developmental benefits in the Pacific.

After three years, working holidaymakers have often formed attachments to people and places and end up applying to stay in Australia as students, partners or temporary skilled workers — a practice unfairly disparaged as “visa hopping.” Removing the option of a third visa would have countered this tendency in keeping with the government’s desire to cut net overseas migration.

Instead of a simple and coherent reform, though, we got another example of administrative tinkering to go with Burke’s direction to Home Affairs to process applications for visas lodged in Australia ahead of those lodged overseas. This reduces net overseas migration in the short term because the person getting the visa is already here.

This might look like an innocuous bureaucratic tweak, but pushing offshore applicants to the back of the queue can have profound effects. Partners, skilled workers and other hopeful migrants are left in limbo, suffering an indefinite wait for a visa.

We might think visa delays are little more than inconvenience for young, footloose “backpackers,” but that’s a misconception. Because previous changes enabled working holidaymakers to extend their stay for three years, many applicants now apply for the visa with that intention, especially when other options are prohibitively expensive and slow.

Online discussion forums are full of accounts of working holidaymakers caught out by Burke’s changes. Among them is Davide, a 32-year-old nurse trained in Italy who has built a career working in large public hospitals in London, where he gained UK citizenship.

In London, he met his Australian boyfriend, Jake. The couple have been together four years and decided to try life together in Sydney. A working holiday visa was a far better option than an $11,710 partner visa that can take years to process.

Besides, he was also wary of committing to Australia without trying it out first. “I visited once to Sydney,” he told me. “It’s really nice and I could see myself living there, but maybe it’s not the right place for me.”

Davide applied for his working holiday visa in July using his UK passport and was booked to fly to Sydney in September. “I know they say not to book flights until you’ve got your visa, but I based my decision on the processing times they put on the Home Affairs website,” he says. “Everybody I talked to said it takes a maximum of two weeks to get a visa, so I was quite relaxed about it.”

Davide went back to his hometown in Italy to say goodbye to family and friends before making the move to Australia. Four months after applying, he’s still there waiting for his visa, and running through his savings.

“It’s quite difficult. If I’d known that it would take this long, then I would have stayed in my job in London,” he says. “If I knew it was going to take another four months, then I could organise my life. I’d consider going back to London to get a temporary job.”
Like many others, he is collateral damage in the government’s clumsy attempt to rein in net overseas migration. •
